Trump says US does not need Iran deal, directs Vance to focus on domestic corruption Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 23:55 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 23:55 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

President Donald Trump said on Thursday the US does not need a deal with Iran and directed Vice President JD Vance, who has played a role in efforts to resolve the war, to focus "his complete and total attention" on alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states. Trump's directive came a day after the Wall Street Journal reported that Vance was considering face-to-face peace talks with a hard-line Iranian security official and a week after the vice president blamed the costly war with Iran for Republicans' midterm elections drubbing. "We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!" Trump wrote on social media, referring to the Strait of Hormuz. Trump had suggested in recent weeks that Iran would be more willing to strike a deal in the eight-month conflict after the US elections, but his administration this week signaled it believes its blockade and economic sanctions against Iran are working, meaning neither a military escalation nor diplomacy is needed. The US military is imposing a blockade on Iranian ports, while attempting to secure safe passage for international shipping through the vital Strait of Hormuz. Iran's military said on Thursday four oil tankers were hit by explosions after they ignored Iranian warnings. Vance's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. VANCE HAD LED IRAN DIPLOMACY Vance, long seen as skeptical of the war the US and Israel launched on Iran in February, led talks with Iranian officials in Pakistan in April that produced a June memorandum of understanding that paused the war but broke down within weeks. Iranian state media said late last month Tehran had received a letter from Vance seeking renewed talks with Washington. Trump said he had not directed his vice president to make the outreach. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Tuesday after talks with US allies in Paris that Iran's demands for a potential deal were "absurd," citing its demand for reparations for the war, and said Trump would not sign a bad deal. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Vance was considering meeting with a senior Iranian security official, a move that would have put Vance at the center of peace negotiations. Reuters has not confirmed the potential talks. Vance, who is viewed as a leading contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, distanced himself from the war last week after Republicans' midterm election rout by Democrats. The vice president blamed the costs of the Iran war in part for the party's losses. He also said an earlier recommendation to end the war was "sound advice." Trump responded to Vance's position by defending the war as necessary to stop Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon. In his social media post, Trump said he had asked Vance to focus instead on a domestic issue the president previously put in his portfolio: leading an effort targeting alleged fraud in Democratic-run cities and states throughout the US. "Our Budget could be quickly BALANCED with the correction of this large-scale criminal activity. CORRUPTION is in the Democrat Leadership’s blood!" Trump wrote on Thursday.

item.content:encoded:
WRAPUP 2-US labor market resilient; existing home sales hit more than 16-year low in October Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 23:19 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 23:19 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits increased more than expected last week, but remained at a level consistent with a stable labor market, allowing the Federal Reserve to focus on fighting inflation. Economists expect layoffs to remain low through the end of the year, though seasonal volatility related to the holiday season could cause some spikes in the claims data. The government last week reported a surge in nonfarm payrolls in October and a decline in the unemployment rate to 4.1% from 4.2% in September. The resilience in the labor market is despite the ongoing Middle East conflict, which is boosting inflation. "Firms are continuing to hold on to labor," said Olivia Cross, senior US economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics. "We expect layoffs to remain low through the fourth quarter, but then come under some pressure next year in response to the recent tightening of financial conditions and the growing use of AI by firms." Initial claims for state unemployment benefits rose 9,000 to a seasonally adjusted 200,000 for the week ended November 7, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 195,000 claims for the latest week. Claims have stayed at or below 200,000 since mid-September and remain close to the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, the lowest since 1969, raising the prospect that the labor market could be tightening. But with wages growing at a moderate pace, most economists do not believe that is the case. Some argue that a smaller workforce, due to retirements and the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, is the key driver of the historically low level of claims. "A generally smaller labor force could mean fewer workers to file for unemployment insurance," said Veronica Clark, an economist at Citigroup. "Of course, this would still be consistent with a low unemployment rate, with continuing claims suggesting the unemployment rate may even fall further towards around 4.0% in data by early 2027." The claims report showed that the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, fell 20,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.697 million during the week ended October 31. But the so-called continuing claims do not include some unemployed people, such as recent college graduates and others who have little or no work history. Some people might also have exhausted their eligibility for benefits, limited to 26 weeks in most states, keeping continuing claims at relatively low levels. The median duration of unemployment jumped to 11.9 weeks in October, the longest since November 2021, from 11.5 weeks in September. Though businesses have been hoarding workers, they have remained reluctant to increase headcount, with economists citing uncertainty from the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its ninth month. Businesses were also unsure of their staffing needs as they embraced AI. US central bank Governor Michael Barr warned on Thursday the nation should be prepared for "serious short-term disruptions" to the job market because of AI, which he said, depending on how fast it is deployed, could begin displacing workers at scale and widening inequality in favor of investors. Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit and rising oil prices following comments by President Donald Trump that the US did not need a deal with Iran weighed on sentiment. The dollar advanced against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields rose. HOUSE PRICES STILL ELEVATED Government data this week showed consumer prices increasing faster than expected in October. That, together with comments from Fed Governor Christopher Waller, prompted financial markets to almost fully price in a 25-basis-point rate hike in December, and to anticipate another increase in January. The Fed left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range last month. While the labor market continues to hold up, rising mortgage rates stemming from the Iran war are depressing the interest-rate-sensitive housing market. Sales of previously owned homes tumbled 5.5% in October to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million units, the National Association of Realtors said in a separate report. That was the lowest level since August 2010, when sales were declining as a homebuyers tax credit ended. The incentive was aimed at stimulating demand following the 2008 global financial crisis. Economists had forecast home resales falling to a rate of 3.85 million units. Sales plunged 8.8% on a year-over-year basis in October. The drop in sales was across all price categories, including those priced $1 million and above, which had experienced strong growth in prior months. The 30-year fixed mortgage rate jumped above 7% in late August, rising to 7.40% by mid-September, for a total of 142 basis points since the US and Israel attacked Iran at the end of February, data from mortgage finance agency Freddie Mac showed. It averaged 7.11% in the latest week, down from 7.18% in the prior week. "Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023," said Lawrence Yun, the NAR's chief economist. The NAR's Housing Affordability Index dropped to 100.7 from 107.3 in October 2025. Existing housing inventory increased 1.3% to 1.590 million units, the highest level since November 2019. Supply rose 4.6% from a year ago. At October's sales pace, it would take 5.1 months to exhaust the current inventory of existing homes, the most since November 2015. That was up from 4.4 months a year ago. The median existing home price last month advanced 0.4% from a year ago to $421,900, the highest for any October. First-time buyers accounted for 29% of sales, down from 32% a year ago. A 40% share in this category is needed for a robust housing market. The housing market weakness is demand-related, with higher prices keeping distressed sales at a negligible 2%. "With mortgage rates expected to remain above 7% through most of 2027, we expect home sales to remain below 4 million until late next year," said Nancy Vanden Houten, lead US economist at Oxford Economics.

item.content:encoded:
NATO will not hold summit in Tirana next year, Albania's Rama says  Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 23:08 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 23:08 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

NATO will not hold a summit in Albania next year despite previous plans to do so, Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said on Thursday. Reuters reported in June that plans for an alliance summit in Albania next year had been thrown into doubt due to resistance from the Trump administration and dissatisfaction among NATO members with Tirana's low defence spending. Speaking in Dublin ahead of a gathering of European leaders, Rama said: “The issue is that there is not yet common position on when the summit will happen, for sure not in 2027." He added: “And in 2028, if it will be a summit, it will be in Tirana." NATO has been considering ending its recent practice of holding annual summits, a move that could avoid a potentially tense encounter with US President Donald Trump later in his term. However, diplomats say the alliance could still decide to hold a summit at short notice in 2026 — but not in Tirana. A NATO official said on Thursday that "the next NATO Summit will be held in Albania. A decision on the date has yet to be made." In a declaration adopted at the June 2025 NATO summit in The Hague, the alliance’s leaders wrote: “We look forward to our next meeting in Turkiye in 2026 followed by a meeting in Albania.” But in a declaration adopted at the alliance’s Ankara summit in July of this year, leaders said, “We look forward to our next meeting,” without specifying a time or location for a future summit.

item.content:encoded:
US STOCKS-Wall St recovers as energy shares climb; Nvidia woes deepen Reuters | Updated: 12-11-2026 22:44 IST | Created: 12-11-2026 22:44 IST

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Wall Street's main indexes staged a turnaround on Thursday after higher oil prices lifted energy shares even as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's exit stirred concerns about the future of the AI heavyweight. The chip giant's shares were last down 4.2%, having bounced off session lows. Retail investors bought Nvidia shares worth about $111 million in the first half hour of trading, the biggest opening bid on record for the stock, according to data from Vanda Analytics. Eight of the 11 major S&P 500 sector indexes were in positive territory, with energy leading gains with a 1.3% jump. Oil prices rose after US President Donald Trump said "we don't need a deal with Iran." At 11:38 a.m. ET, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 125.85 points, or 0.24%, to 52,612.34, the S&P 500 added 13.09 points, or 0.17%, to 7,632.47 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 34.77 points, or 0.14%, to 25,500.96. "We've spent two years in a market where the indexes sat at record highs while most of the companies inside them traded well below theirs," said Bill Mann, chief investment strategist at Motley Fool Asset Management. "A rally that doesn't depend on a handful of names is the first thing we'd want to see if that's going to change." AI TRADE IN CONFUSION Still, some investors warned that questions will persist about the future of AI companies that have deep ties with Nvidia. The company has backed several firms, including its own customers, through financing arrangements that now face greater scrutiny after Huang's departure. "Nvidia doesn't just sell chips. It also stands behind some of the financing that helps customers build the data centers those chips go into," said Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management. "How much demand comes from customers who can pay on their own? How much needs an Nvidia investment or guarantee? And what happens to profits if that support gets more expensive?" The Philadelphia Semiconductor index rose 0.2%. Neocloud company Nebius said its 2026 revenue would come in at the low end of its previous forecast, pulling its shares down 17%. Peer CoreWeave dropped about 6%. Other data center-related firms IREN and Applied Digital fell 5% and 4%, respectively. However, shares of some Magnificent Seven firms advanced, with Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon up over 1% each. Nvidia's rivals Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom were up over 6% each. INFLATION DATA AWAITED, OIL RISES Investors are also awaiting the release of the Producer Price Index on Friday, which will follow a hotter-than-expected consumer price reading earlier this week. Traders see a December rate hike by the Federal Reserve as a certainty, with about an 8% chance of an outsized 50-basis-point increase, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack said she does not believe that the central bank needs to shift to more aggressive rate rises to combat inflation. Separately, Michael Saylor's Strategy fell 3.7% after index operator MSCI said it will remove the stock from its global indexes. Declining issues outnumbered advancers by a 2.15-to-1 ratio on the NYSE, and by a 2.31-to-1 ratio on the Nasdaq. The S&P 500 posted 18 new 52-week highs and 2 new lows while the Nasdaq Composite recorded 35 new highs and 173 new lows.
